overview: The atlas assigns Denmark-Norway to 1000 to 1100, so this card explains early medieval Danish and Norwegian connections. It must not be read as the much later union’s founding date. Rule and alliances changed repeatedly, while ships, crafts and money linked communities across the sea.

periods.title: Changing rulers and claims
periods.summary: Danish influence in Norway varied; one map label cannot establish a continuous century-long union.

periods.title: Cnut’s Norwegian rule
periods.summary: Cnut gained control of Norway in 1028; Norwegian leaders chose Magnus in 1035.

periods.title: Distinct political histories, continued exchange
periods.summary: Political separation did not remove the sea routes and working connections between communities.

items.text: Cnut became king of Denmark in 1018 and gained Norway in 1028, while also ruling England. Managing several kingdoms involved representatives, diplomacy and gifts as well as force. His personal power did not create one uniform society.

A Danish silver penny in the British Museum, dated 1019 to 1035, uses a portrait and cross closely related to an English design. Money can reveal imitation and adaptation across kingdoms, rather than a separate national invention in each place.

sections.title: Ships carried work as well as warriors

items.text: Skuldelev 1 was a cargo vessel built in western Norway around 1030. Its heavy pine planks and broad form suited carrying substantial loads. A vessel’s practical design helps distinguish transporting goods from the demands of a fast warship.

The same vessel was repaired using oak near the Oslofjord and eastern Denmark. Repair timber records a working life across different places. A ship could outlast its first crew’s plans and become a patchwork of skilled maintenance.

Skuldelev 3, built from Danish oak around 1040, carried goods in coastal waters. Loose deck planks covered the ends, leaving an open central hold. Its layout made room for cargo while preserving space for handling the vessel.

The museum suggests that Skuldelev 3 could have carried an owner with associates or family to markets or assemblies. This is a plausible interpretation of its capacity, not a passenger list recovered from the ship.

Making Ottar’s modern experimental wool sail drew on textile researchers and the wool of about 200 small sheep. That figure belongs to the reconstruction project. It makes the large amount of textile work behind sailing visible without inventing an ancient production total.

Viking-period combs, tweezers and ear picks survive in archaeological collections. Some combs had protective cases. These objects show attention to personal grooming, although they cannot prove that every person followed the same bathing schedule.

Spinning, weaving and sewing required sustained work. The museum interprets complicated textile techniques as evidence that some women specialized in production. That is more specific than imagining all clothing as a quick extra task after the other household jobs.

Keys are often presented as the universal badge of a Viking housewife. The museum cautions that they are actually rare among female grave goods. A memorable symbol should be checked against the whole archaeological sample.

CNVT REX DANOR means “Cnut, king of the Danes.” This Latin title appears on a coin type from Lund dated 1082 to 1084, illustrated in the Royal Blood study. Its ruler is Cnut the Holy, a later king than Cnut the Great.

The reverse of that coin type names a moneyer and mint. The study identifies many moneyers associated with its production. Coin legends could preserve the work of named specialists as well as the ruler whose authority they advertised.

ending.text: Cnut’s Norwegian rule ended in the changes around 1035; Danish and Norwegian histories continued through other rulers and later unions. The atlas’s 1100 endpoint is not a single political collapse. Its imported name and very broad polygon require caution and do not verify sovereignty over every shaded place.

sources.title: National Museum of Denmark: Cnut the Great
sources.note: Danish kingship from 1018, Norwegian takeover in 1028 and Norwegian choice of Magnus in 1035; dates do not support a continuous 1000 to 1100 union.

sources.title: National Museum of Denmark: The extent of Viking-period Denmark
sources.note: Danish claims and varying control in Norway between 970 and 1035; historical borders were not fixed modern national outlines.

sources.title: Viking Ship Museum: Skuldelev 1
sources.note: Norwegian-built cargo ship, heavy pine planks and later repairs with oak; possible trading range distinguished from a proven voyage.

sources.title: Viking Ship Museum: Ottar reconstruction
sources.note: Original Skuldelev 1 built around 1030; modern reconstruction and experimental wool sail. Sheep numbers describe the modern project, not an ancient account.

sources.title: Viking Ship Museum: Skuldelev 3
sources.note: Danish oak coastal trader around 1040, open cargo hold, sail and oars; proposed market and assembly journeys.

sources.title: National Museum of Denmark: Appearance
sources.note: Archaeological grooming equipment. Generalized stories about weekly bathing and attraction are not used as universal customs.

sources.title: National Museum of Denmark: Women in the Viking Age
sources.note: Textile work and specialist production; keys in female graves are rarer than a familiar household stereotype suggests. Broad claims of equal rights are not adopted.

sources.note: Silver penny dated 1019 to 1035; bust and cross; curator compares its design with Æthelred II’s coinage.
